2.text: The poorest of the larger reindeer-skins, those not fit for any other purpose,

3.text: are clipped of hair with a sharp knife, and then cut into a narrow strip less

4.text: than half and inch broad. The skins are cut when fresh, or, if dry, they are

5.text: dipped in water to make them softer and more pliable. The line is stretched

6.text: out of doors, made as taut as possible, and allowed to dry. This kind of line is

7.text: called a “leather line” (ñilhɪˊlhɪn). Among the Reindeer Chukchee it is used

8.text: for almost every kind of lashing. The best line of this kind is made of the

9.text: skin of old wild reindeer-bucks. The neck part is so thick that it might be

10.text: used for boot-soles, and the line made of it is quite strong. When plaited, it

11.text: is used for lassos (see Fig. 162, a). The Maritime Chukchee prepare a similar

12.text: kind of thin line of the skins of smaller seals. It is called “seal-skin leather”

13.text: (mêmɪčêˊčhɪn), and it is better in quality than the reindeer-skin line.

14.text: The skill of the natives in cutting the skin into narrow lines is very

15.text: remarkable. Usually one man holds the hide and the line near the cut, and

16.text: pulls them toward himself, while another makes the cut by steadily drawing

17.text: towards himself a knife held in an upright position. For a hundred feet of

18.text: line the hand of the cutter will not change its regular motion or swerve from

19.text: the proper direction. The entire line seems of exactly the same width.

20.text: Stouter line is made of the skin of the ground-seal and of walrus-hide.

21.text: These are cut in the manner described, either fresh or dry. The line is usually

22.text: from an inch to an inch and a half broad. The line made of ground-seal

23.text: skin (uᵋnečiˊčhɪn, “ground-seal leather”) is best in quality. That

25.text: with moisture, and wears out more rapidly. The hide of young

26.text: walrus gives a line of much better quality. The ground-seal skin

27.text: line is often dyed black with soot mixed with oil, to make it

28.text: stand the dampness better. When freshly cut and dried, the line

29.text: is almost as hard as wood. To make it more pliable it has to

30.text: be chewed all over, in which process it usually increases in breadth.

31.text: After that, it is drawn with considerable force across the edge

32.text: of some immovable object, like the runner of a heavily loaded

33.text: sledge or one of the larger tent-poles. A special implement of

34.text: bone or antler is sometimes used in this process (Fig. 161).

35.text: It contains a hole with sharp edges, through which the line is

36.text: repeatedly drawn. By means of another hole in the top, the

37.text: implement is suspended from the house-frame.

38.text: For lassos, tent-ropes, and various kinds of cord, the Rein-

39.text: deer Chukchee and the Lamut often use thin plaited “leather

40.text: line” (Fig. 162, a) or plaited sinew (Fig. 162, b). The sinew
